'''Arnold Thackray''' (born 30 July 1939) is an [[emeritus professor]] at the [[University of Pennsylvania]]. He has held academic positions at  institutions, including a visiting fellowship at [[All Souls College]], Oxford, and a fellowship at [[Churchill College, Cambridge]].<ref name="DexterBio">{{cite web |date=2006 |title=Arnold Thackray (1939–) |url=https://acshist.scs.illinois.edu/awards/Dexter%20Papers/ThackrayDexterBioJJB.pdf |access-date=31 May 2023 |website=American Chemical Society Division of the History of Chemistry}}</ref> He has also taught at the [[List of people associated with the London School of Economics|London School of Economics]], [[Harvard University]], the [[Institute for Advanced Study]], the [[Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences]] at Stanford, and the [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |title=Celebrating 50 years of the Department of History and Sociology of Science at the University of Pennsylvania |url=https://hssonline.org/blogpost/1987463/479514/Celebrating-50-years-of-the-Department-of-History-and-Sociology-of-Science-at-the-University-of-Pennsylvania |work=History of Science Society}}</ref>

He was the founding chair of the Department of History and Sociology of Science and now holds the title of Joseph Priestley Professor Emeritus.

Thackray was the founding director of the institution originally established as the Chemical Heritage Foundation, now known as the [[Science History Institute]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Reisch |first=Marc S. |date=2025-01-21 |title=History In the Making |url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/92/i46/HISTORY-MAKING.html |access-date=2025-07-22 |website=Chemical & Engineering News |language=en}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Thackray was born in [[Manchester]] [[England]] on 30 July 1939.<ref>Confirmed in a conversation with Arnold Thackray 30 May 2023</ref><ref name="MGS">{{cite web |title=Spotlight on Old Mancunians: Arnold Thackray {{!}} Manchester Grammar School |url=https://www.mgs-life.co.uk/article/spotlight-on-old-mancunians-arnold-thackray?ref=71 |website=Manchester Grammar School |access-date=31 May 2023}}</ref>

At the age of 10, he was awarded a Foundation Scholarship to attend [[Manchester Grammar School]].<ref name="MGS" />

He earned a Bachelor of Science degree with First Class Honours in chemistry from the [[University of Bristol]] in 1960.<ref name="DexterBio" /> After graduation, he began working in industry in [[Yorkshire]]. During this time, he became involved with a group at [[University of Leeds|Leeds University]], led by [[Jerome Ravetz]], that explored emerging ideas in the history of science.<ref name=":0" />

Ravetz encouraged Thackray to apply to the fledging [[doctoral program]] in [[history of science]] at [[Cambridge University]].<ref name=":0" /> In October 1963 Thackray  entered recently established [[Churchill College, Cambridge|Churchill College, Cambridge University]].<ref name="CIB" /> Under the direction of [[Mary Hesse]], a leader in the field of [[philosophy of science]],<ref name="CIB">{{cite journal|last1=Baykoucheva|first1=Svetia|title=The Chemical Heritage Foundation: Past, Present, and Future|journal=Chemical Information Bulletin|date=Fall 2008|volume=60|issue=2|pages=10–13|url=http://www.acscinf.org/content/chemical-heritage-foundation-past-present-and-future|access-date=30 April 2017|archive-date=24 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180324224619/http://www.acscinf.org/content/chemical-heritage-foundation-past-present-and-future|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="DexterBio" /> he earned his [[Doctorate of Philosophy]] degree in 1966.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Arnold Thackray |url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/profile/arnold-thackray/ |access-date=2025-07-22 |website=Science History Institute |language=en-US}}</ref>

A year earlier, Thackray had already become the first graduate student at [[Churchill College]] to be elected a Fellow of the college.<ref name="MGS" /> In this new role, he pioneered the effort to secure the papers of leading British scientists including Sir James Chadwick,  for what in 1973 would become the Churchill College Archive Centre.<ref name="about">{{cite book |last1=Thackray |first1=Arnold |title=John Dalton Critical Assessments of his life and science |date=1972 |publisher=Harvard University Press |location=Cambridge Mass |isbn=0674475259 |chapter=About the author |url=https://archive.org/details/trent_0116301348631}}</ref>

==Academic and professional career==
Thackray decided to seek his BTA—his 'been to America' degree. In September 1967 he intermitted his Fellowship to accept a one-year visiting lectureship at Harvard University, fully intending to return to the original Cambridge.<ref name="about"/> However, enjoying American academe, in 1968 he chose to join the faculty of the [[University of Pennsylvania]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Times |first=Robert Reinhold Special to The New York |date=1970-02-18 |title=Rise of History of Science Is a Reply to Technology |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1970/02/18/archives/rise-of-history-of-science-is-a-reply-to-technology-rise-of-history.html |access-date=2025-07-22 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

In 1969 he became director of a joint Penn-Bryn Mawr-American Philosophical Society graduate program in the history of medicine and the biological sciences.<ref name="DexterBio" /> In 1970 he became chairman of Penn's Department of the History and Philosophy of Science, which soon thereafter was renamed the Department of the History and Sociology of Science in order to be more consistent with the direction that Thackray had chosen for it.<ref name="about" /><ref name="PennBio">{{cite web |title=Arnold Thackray {{!}} History and Sociology of Science |url=https://hss.sas.upenn.edu/people/arnold-thackray |website=History and Sociology of Science |access-date=31 May 2023}}</ref> As chairman of the brand-new HSS Department, Thackray drew on [[Faculty (academic staff)|faculty]] members from such disciplinary areas of the university as history, philosophy, anthropology, sociology, chemistry, physics, biology, engineering, English, and American civilization.<ref name="Department">{{cite web|url=https://hss.sas.upenn.edu/about|title=Department History|website=hss.sas.upenn.edu|publisher=University of Pennsylvania|access-date=6 May 2017}}</ref>

Thackray was a member of the Penn faculty for 28 years, retiring in 1996 as Joseph Priestley Professor emeritus.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Martin |first=Caitlin |date=2022-10-27 |title=The Power of a Teacher |url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/collections/blog/the-power-of-a-teacher/ |access-date=2025-07-22 |website=Science History Institute |language=en-US}}</ref>

His academic [[research]] has focused on the rise of modern science since the death of  [[Isaac Newton]], and on the interactions between the [[scientific community]] and society as a whole.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Thackray |first=Arnold |date=1985-01-01 |title=The Historian and the Progress of Science* |url=https://doi.org/10.1177/016224398501000104 |journal=Science, Technology, & Human Values |language=EN |volume=10 |issue=1 |pages=17–27 |doi=10.1177/016224398501000104 |issn=0162-2439|url-access=subscription }}</ref> He has mentored twenty PhD students and authored or edited a wide variety of scholarly books and articles. Additionally, he has been a member of the History of Science Society Executive Committee and [[editor]] of [[Isis]] and the HSS Newsletter (1978-1985), while also relaunching and editing [[Osiris]] (1984-1994).  Additionally, Thackray has held visiting professorships at [[Bryn Mawr College]] (1968 through 1973), the [[London School of Economics]] (1971-1972), the [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]] (1978),<ref name="DexterBio" /> in addition to the [[Institute for Advanced Study]], Princeton, NJ (1980), and the [[Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences]], Palo Alto, CA (1974 and 1984).<ref name="about" />

He also served as an Executive Committee member and Treasurer of the [[American Council of Learned Societies]] (1985-1995).<ref name="DexterBio" /> He was one of the four co-founders of, and the 1982-83 President of, the [[Society for Social Studies of Science]]. He also participated on many review committees and advisory boards, such as those of the [[John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation]] and the [[National Science Foundation]]. In his years at Penn, Arnold Thackray additionally served as [[curator]] of The Edgar Fahs Smith Memorial Collection in the History of Chemistry.<ref name="PSU">{{cite web|last1=Manning|first1=Kenneth|title=A History of Chemistry|url=http://pabook2.libraries.psu.edu/palitmap/EFSmith.html|publisher=Pennsylvania Center for the Book|access-date=7 May 2017|archive-date=27 May 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180527201349/http://pabook2.libraries.psu.edu/palitmap/EFSmith.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

=== Chemical Heritage Foundation ===
A 1979-1980 task force led by chemist/historian John H. Wotiz<ref name="Wotiz">{{cite web|title=John H. Wotiz (1919–2001)|url=https://www.scs.illinois.edu/~mainzv/HIST/awards/Dexter%20Papers/WotizDexterBioJJB.pdf|website=American Chemical Society, Division of the History of Chemistry|publisher=American Chemical Society Dexter Awards|access-date=27 May 2017}}</ref> resulted in a recommendation to the [[American Chemical Society]] that it create a center for the history of chemistry.<ref name="CHOC1983">{{cite journal|title=Center for History of Chemistry Inaugural|journal=CHOC News|date=Summer 1983|volume=1|issue=3|pages=1–5}}</ref>  In 1981, the American Chemical Society solicited proposals to develop such a center.<ref name="CHOC1983" /> Thackray proposed that the center be at the University of Pennsylvania.<ref name="Haas">{{cite web|last1=Gussman |first1=Neil |title=The Power of John C. Haas's Good Name |url=http://www.chemheritage.org/about/history/chf-founders/2011-05-16-john-c-haas.aspx |publisher=Chemical Heritage Foundation |access-date=8 May 2017 |url-status=bot: unknown |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160712182325/http://www.chemheritage.org/about/history/chf-founders/2011-05-16-john-c-haas.aspx |archive-date=12 July 2016 }}</ref><ref name="CHOC1983" /><ref name="CandENews1987">{{cite journal|last1=Carpenter|first1=Ernest|title=Chemistry History Center Receives Large Grant|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=November 16, 1987|volume=65|issue=46|page=6}}</ref> Late in 1983, the [[American Institute of Chemical Engineers]] (AIChE) became a co-sponsor.<ref name="CHOC1984">{{cite journal|title=American Institute of Chemical Engineers Joins CHOC Endeavor|journal=CHOC News|date=Spring 1984|volume=2|issue=1|pages=1–3}}</ref>

In 1987 CHOC was promised its first [[Financial endowment|endowment]].<ref name="CandENews1987" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/history|title = History |website=Science History Institute |date = 31 May 2016}}</ref>

Thackray sought to move CHF to a home of its own somewhere in the greater Philadelphia (Wilmington, DE to Princeton, NJ) area. In 1993 CHF purchased the [[First National Bank (Philadelphia)|First National Bank]], which stood in the backyard of [[Benjamin Franklin]]'s home, within what by the 1980s had become Philadelphia's Independence National Park. The build-out of this 1865 structure into a modern 120,000 sq. ft. facility took over a decade of planning and fundraising. 
The repurposed complex eventually included offices, archives, and space for the Othmer Library (itself steadily growing in size and stature as an internationally-acclaimed resource). The home of CHF would eventually include a capacious public museum  designed by [[Ralph Appelbaum]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Philadelphia's Chemical Heritage Foundation Features Digital Signage Media Column |url=https://digitalsignageuniverse.typepad.com/digital_signage_universe/2012/04/philadelphias-chemical-heritage-foundation-features-digital-signage-media-column.html |work=Digital Signage Universe |date=April 24, 2012}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/distillations/magazine/making-modernity-a-gallery-preview|title = Making Modernity: A Gallery Preview|date = 23 March 2008}}</ref> The overall project was complete in 2008.<ref name="C&ENews2008">{{cite journal|last1=Arnaud|first1=Celia Henry|title=The Art of Science|journal=Chemical and Engineering News|date=October 27, 2008|volume=86|issue=43|pages=34–36|doi=10.1021/cen-v086n043.p034}}</ref>
Under Thackray's tenure, CHF steadily expanded its scope, its sponsoring organizations, its repertoire of visiting academic scholars, and its activities around the country and overseas.<ref>bArnaud, Celia Henry (27 October 2008). "The Art of Science". Chemical and Engineering News. 86 (43): 34–36. doi:10.1021/cen-v086n043.p034</ref> An annual [[Othmer Gold Medal]] was inaugurated in 1997, to honor individuals contributing to science through innovation, entrepreneurship, research, legislation, and philanthropy. The Award’s four sponsors were the ACS, the AIChE, [[The Chemists' Club]], and the [[Société de Chimie Industrielle (American Section)]]. A growing series of other medals and prizes followed, in partnership with relevant organizations in the USA and abroad, to honor pioneers in fields ranging from materials science to biotechnology.<ref name="REISCH">{{cite journal |last1=REISCH |first1=MARC |title=CHF Hosts Multiple Celebrations |journal=Chemical & Engineering News |date=August 5, 2002 |volume=80 |issue=31 |page=49 |doi=10.1021/cen-v080n031.p049 |url=https://pubsapp.acs.org/cen/acsnews/8031/8031acsn.html|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="OthmerMedal">{{cite web|title=Othmer Gold Medal|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/othmer-gold-medal|access-date=22 March 2018|website=[[Science History Institute]]|date=31 May 2016}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/affiliate-partnership-awards|title = Affiliate Partnership Awards|date = 31 May 2016}}</ref>

Thackray served as president of CHF until 2009, after which time he served a seven-year term as Chancellor. Over the 28 years of his active leadership of a growing organization, he raised a permanent endowment of $130 million, while investing almost $50 million to create CHF’s home.<ref name=CEN2007>{{cite journal|last=Reisch|first=Marc S.|title=Haverford College President Thomas Tritton Will Take CHF Helm in January|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=2007-06-25|volume=85|issue=26|page=11|doi=10.1021/cen-v085n026.p011a |url=http://www.chemheritage.org/about/news-and-press/chf-in-the-media/2007-6-25-thomas-tritton-will-take-chf-helm.aspx |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20160712194722/http://www.chemheritage.org/about/news-and-press/chf-in-the-media/2007-6-25-thomas-tritton-will-take-chf-helm.aspx|archivedate=July 12, 2016|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name="AAAS">{{cite web |title=Arnold Wilfrid Thackray |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/arnold-wilfrid-thackray |website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences |access-date=31 May 2023 |language=en |date=25 April 2023}}</ref>

=== Life Sciences Foundation ===
After stepping down as president of CHF, Thackray relocated to [[Silicon Valley]]. There he founded the [[Life Sciences Foundation]] .<ref name="BIO">{{cite web |date=April 12, 2012 |title=The Life Sciences Foundation – Telling the Story of Biotechnology {{!}} BIO |url=https://www.bio.org/blogs/life-sciences-foundation-telling-story-biotechnology |access-date=31 May 2023 |website=www.bio.org |language=en}}</ref> The foundation was conceived at a 2009 meeting with four biotechnology industry leaders. The group reasoned that biotech, by then 40 years old, had a poorly understood history.<ref name="LSF_2014">{{citation | url=https://globenewswire.com/news-release/2014/07/02/648453/10088040/en/Life-Sciences-Foundation-Appoints-Carl-Feldbaum-as-New-Board-Chair.html#sthash.k40ggRnf.dpuf |title=Life Sciences Foundation Appoints Carl Feldbaum as New Board Chair |date=July 2, 2014 |access-date=July 19, 2015 |work=Life Sciences Foundation via Globe Newswire|location=San Francisco}}</ref> The Life Sciences Foundation was formed in 2011 to capture the stories of the industry’s founders, while increasing awareness of the field’s significance through oral histories, public events, and a variety of publications, including a free magazine.<ref name="Bioworld">{{cite journal|last1=Morrison|first1=Trista|title=Life Sciences Foundation Looks to Capture History of Biotech|journal=BioWorld Today|date=February 2, 2012|volume=23|issue=22|page=1}}</ref><ref name="Inquirer2015">{{cite news|last1=Brubaker|first1=Harold|title=Chemical Heritage and Life Sciences foundations merging|url=https://www.philly.com/philly/business/20151015_Chemical_heritage_and_life_sciences_foundations_merging.html|access-date=2 May 2017|agency=Philadelphia Inquirer|date=October 15, 2015}}</ref><ref name="Salisbury">{{cite news|last1=Salisbury|first1=Stephan|title=Chemical Heritage Foundation is morphing into the Science History Institute|url=http://www.philly.com/philly/entertainment/arts/chemical-heritage-foundation-science-history-institute-philadelphia-20Inquirer|date=January 3, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Chemical Heritage and Life Sciences foundations merging |url=https://www.philly.com/philly/business/20151015_Chemical_heritage_and_life_sciences_foundations_merging.html|access-date=2 May 2017|agency=Philadelphia Inquirer|date=October 15, 2015}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
Thackray was the 1983 recipient of the [[Dexter Award]] of the American Chemical Society for his work on the [[history of chemistry]].<ref name="Dexter">{{cite web|title=Dexter Award for Outstanding Achievement in the History of Chemistry|url=https://www.scs.illinois.edu/~mainzv/HIST/awards/dexter.php|website=scs.illinois.edu|publisher=American Chemical Society|access-date=30 April 2017}}</ref> In 1984, Thackray received the George Sarton Memorial Lecturer Award at the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] with a presentation entitled "The Historian's Calling in the Age of Science".<ref name="HSS">{{cite web|title=George Sarton Memorial Lecture|url=https://hssonline.org/about/honors/george-sarton-memorial-lecture/|website=hssonline.org|publisher=History of Science Society|access-date=4 May 2017}}</ref> He was twice awarded fellowships from the [[John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation]] (1971 and 1985).<ref name="DexterBio" /> Thackray is a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the [[Royal Historical Society]] and the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] Sigma XI, and the American Chemical Society, which sponsored a [[Academic conference|symposium]] in his honor in 2009.<ref name="ACS2009">{{cite book |title=American Chemical Society Division of the History of Chemistry Program and Abstracts 238th ACS National Meeting Washington, DC |date=2009 |publisher=American Chemical Society |page=13 |url=https://acshist.scs.illinois.edu/meetings/2009-fall/HIST%20Fall%202009%20Program%20Abstracts%20Only.pdf}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Thackray became a citizen of the [[United States]] in 1981.<ref name="DexterBio" /> He first married Barbara (née Hughes) Thackray, a physicist who became a teacher at the [[Shipley School]] in [[Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania|Bryn Mawr]], [[Pennsylvania]].<ref name="NYT2002">{{cite news|title=Weddings; Helen Thackray, Lawrence Kessner| work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/05/19/style/weddings-helen-thackray-lawrence-kessner.html?emc=eta1|access-date=30 April 2017|agency=New York Times|date=May 19, 2002}}</ref> He is the father of Helen Thackray, a biotechnology executive.<ref name="NYT2002"/><ref name="Jenkins">{{cite news |last1=Jenkins |first1=Kristina M. |title=Helen Thackray '86: Developing Treatments through Biotechnology |url=https://www.shipleyschool.org/2018-news-detail?pk=1003448 |access-date=26 June 2019 |work=Shipley News |date=November 30, 2015}}</ref>
Thackray's wife since 1994 is Diana (née Schueler) Thackray.<ref name="SCHUELER">{{cite news |title=Obituary OSCAR J. SCHUELER |url=https://www.legacy.com/obituaries/fortwayne/obituary.aspx?n=oscar-j-schueler&pid=2149590 |access-date=26 June 2019 |work=Fort Wayne newspaper |date=April 20, 2004}}</ref>
Walking, gardening, reading, and raising roses have been his hobbies.<ref name="CHOC1983" />
